title: Where the name Son of God comes from
source_text: Ἔλεγε δὴ μετὰ τὰ ἐκκείμενα τοιαῦτα· ὁπόθεν δὲ καὶ αὐτὸ τοῦτο ἐπῆλθεν αὐτοῖς θεοῦ υἱὸν καλεῖν, σημαίνω. ἄνδρες παλαιοὶ τόνδε τὸν κόσμον ὡς ἐκ θεοῦ γενόμενον παῖδά τε αὐτοῦ καὶ ἠΐθεον προσεῖπον. πάνυ γοῦν ὅμοιος οὗτός τε κἀκεῖνος παῖς θεοῦ. ᾠήθη δὴ υἱὸν θεοῦ ἡμᾶς λέγειν, παραποιήσαντας τὰ περὶ τοῦ κόσμου ὡς ἐκ θεοῦ γενομένου καὶ υἱοῦ ὄντος αὐτοῦ καὶ θεοῦ· οὐ γὰρ ἐδυνήθη ἐπιστήσας τοῖς χρόνοις Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν προφητῶν ἰδεῖν ὅτι καθόλου τὸ εἶναί τινα υἱὸν θεοῦ πρὸ Ἑλλήνων καὶ ὧν φησιν ὁ Κέλσος παλαιῶν ἀνδρῶν οἱ παρ᾿ Ἰουδαίοις προφῆται ἐπροφήτευσαν. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ἐβουλήθη τὸ παρὰ Πλάτωνι ἐν ταῖς ἐπιστολαῖς λελεγμένον, οὗ ἐν τοῖς ἀνωτέρω ἐμνήσθημεν, περὶ τοῦ διακοσμήσαντος τόδε τὸ πᾶν ὡς ὄντος υἱοῦ θεοῦ παραθέσθαι· ἵνα μὴ καὶ αὐτὸς ὑπὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος. ον πολλάκις ἐσέμνυνεν, ἀναγκασθῇ παραδέξασθαι ὅτι ὁ μὲν δημιουργὸς τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς υἱός ἐστι τοῦ θεοῦ, ὁ δὲ πρῶτος καὶ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸς πατήρ ἐστιν αὐτοῦ. εἰ δὲ τῷ τηλικούτῳ υἱῷ τοῦ θεοῦ ἡνῶσθαι φάσκοντες τῇ ἄκρᾳ μετοχῇ ἐκείνου τὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ψυχὴν οὐκέτι χωρίζομεν ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνου αὐτὴν, οὐδὲν θαυμαστόν. οἴδασι γὰρ οἱ ἱεροὶ τῶν θείων γραμμάτων λόγοι καὶ ἄλλα, δύο τῇ ἑαυτῶν φύσει τυγχάνοντα, εἰς ἓν ἀλλήλοις εἶναι λελογισμένα καὶ ὄντα. οἷον περὶ μὲν ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς λέλεκται· „οὐκέτι εἰσὶ δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία,“ περὶ δὲ τοῦ τελείου καὶ κολλωμένου τῷ ἀληθινῷ κυρίῳ, λόγῳ καὶ σοφίᾳ καὶ ἀληθείᾳ, ὅτι „ὁ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστιν.“ εἰ δ᾿ „ὁ κολλώμενος τῷ κυρίῳ ἓν πνεῦμά ἐστι.“ τίς μᾶλλον τῆς Ἰησοῦ ψυχῆς ἢ κἂν παραπλησίως κεκόλληται τῷ κυρίῳ, τῷ αὐτολόγῳ καὶ αὐτοσοφίᾳ καὶ αὐτοαληθείᾳ καὶ αὐτοδικαιοσύνῃ; ὅπερ εἰ οὕτως ἔχει, οὐκ εἰσὶ δύο ἡ ψυχὴ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πρὸς τὸν „πάσης κτίσεως“ πρωτότοκον θεὸν λόγον.
pass_a_gloss: He was saying (λέγω) after the things set out (ἔκκειμαι) such things: 'Whence (ὁπόθεν) this very thing came upon (ἐπέρχομαι) them, to call (καλέω) [him] son of God, I indicate (σημαίνω). Ancient men (ἄνδρες παλαιοί) addressed (προσεῖπον) this world (κόσμος), as having come to be (γίγνομαι) from God, his child (παῖς) and youth (ἠΐθεος). Very similar (ὅμοιος) indeed (γοῦν) this one and that one, child of God.' He supposed (οἴομαι) that we say son of God, having distorted (παραποιέω) the things about the world as having come to be from God and being his son (υἱός) and god (θεός); for he was not able, attending (ἐφίστημι) to the times of Moses and the prophets, to see that generally (καθόλου) that there is some son of God, before Greeks and the ancient men he speaks of, the prophets among the Jews prophesied (προφητεύω). But neither did he wish (βούλομαι) to set beside (παρατίθημι) what is said in Plato in the letters (ἐπιστολαί), which we mentioned (μιμνῄσκομαι) above, about the one who ordered (διακοσμέω) this all (τὸ πᾶν) as being son of God; lest he himself too by Plato, whom he often magnified (σεμνύνω), be compelled (ἀναγκάζω) to accept (παραδέχομαι) that the craftsman (δημιουργός) of this all is son of God, and the first (πρῶτος) and over all (ἐπὶ πᾶσι) God is his father (πατήρ). If, saying that the soul (ψυχή) of Jesus has been united (ἑνόω) to so great a son of God by the highest participation (ἄκρα μετοχή) in him, we no longer separate (χωρίζω) it from him, nothing wonderful. For the sacred words of the divine writings (θεῖα γράμματα) know also other things, being two by their own nature (φύσις), reckoned (λογίζομαι) and being into one with each other. As about man and woman it is said: 'no longer are they two but one flesh (σάρξ)'; and about the perfect one (τέλειος) and the one cleaving (κολλάομαι) to the true (ἀληθινός) Lord, Word (λόγος) and Wisdom (σοφία) and Truth (ἀλήθεια), that 'the one cleaving to the Lord is one spirit (πνεῦμα)'. And if 'the one cleaving to the Lord is one spirit', who more than the soul of Jesus, or even comparably (παραπλησίως), has cleaved to the Lord, the Word-itself (αὐτόλογος) and Wisdom-itself (αὐτοσοφία) and Truth-itself (αὐτοαλήθεια) and Righteousness-itself (αὐτοδικαιοσύνη)? Which if it is so, the soul of Jesus and the firstborn (πρωτότοκος) 'of all creation (κτίσις)' God Word are not two.
pass_b_english: After the passages set out above, Celsus went on to say something like this: “I shall show where they got this very idea of calling him Son of God. Men of old called this world the child of God and a youth, since it came into being from him. Very like each other, to be sure, are this child of God and that one!”

He supposed, then, that we speak of a Son of God by twisting what is said about the world, namely that it came into being from God and is his son and a god. For he was not able to attend to the times of Moses and the prophets and see that the prophets among the Jews foretold that there is a Son of God at all, before the Greeks and before those whom Celsus calls men of old. Nor did he wish to quote what is said in Plato’s letters, which we mentioned earlier, about the one who ordered this universe as being the Son of God (Plato, Letter 6, 323d), for fear that he too might be compelled by Plato, whom he often extolled, to accept that the maker of this universe is the Son of God, while the first God, who is over all, is his Father.

And if we say that the soul of Jesus has been united with so great a Son of God by the highest participation in him, and so no longer separate it from him, there is nothing to wonder at. For the sacred words of the divine writings know of other things too which, though two in their own nature, are reckoned as one and are one with each other. For example, it is said of husband and wife, “They are no longer two but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6); and of the perfect man, who is joined to the true Lord, the Word and Wisdom and Truth, that “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17).

But if “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit,” who has been joined to the Lord, to the Word himself, Wisdom himself, Truth himself and Righteousness himself, more than the soul of Jesus, or even nearly as much? If this is so, the soul of Jesus and God the Word, the firstborn “of all creation” (Colossians 1:15), are not two.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words are marked off as his: the three sentences from ὁπόθεν to παῖς θεοῦ (ending ‘that one!’); Koetschau prints no quotation marks, and the boundary at ‘He supposed’ (ᾠήθη) follows the shift from first person to Origen’s third-person report. ἠΐθεος means an unmarried youth; rendered ‘a youth’. The last sentence of Celsus (πάνυ γοῦν ὅμοιος ...) is sarcastic and is rendered as such. Plato reference: the Sixth Letter, 323d, on the God of all and the Father of the leader and cause, which Origen cited earlier in this book (6.8); citation given since Origen says ‘in Plato’s letters’. Source misprint ον for ὃν (‘whom he often extolled’). Matthew 19:6 (also Mark 10:8) for ‘no longer two but one flesh’. The titles Word, Wisdom, Truth and Righteousness echo John 1:1, 1 Corinthians 1:24, John 14:6 and 1 Corinthians 1:30; left uncited inline as titles rather than quotations. αὐτόλογος etc. rendered ‘the Word himself’, ‘Wisdom himself’ and so on, since they name Christ.
Celsus: 'where this very idea ... came to them from' -> 'where they got this very idea' (ὁπόθεν ... ἐπῆλθεν αὐτοῖς; stiff end-preposition removed)

Celsus: 'called this world, since it came into being from God, his child and a youth' -> 'called this world the child of God and a youth, since it came into being from him' (Greek order unwound; sense unchanged)
'he could not, by attending to the times ..., see' -> 'he was not able to attend to the times ... and see' (οὐκ ἐδυνήθη governs ἐπιστήσας too; old wording implied he did attend)
'He did not wish it lest he too should be compelled' -> 'for fear that he too might be compelled' (one ἵνα μή clause, no added repeated verb)
Speaker boundary checked: Celsus = ὁπόθεν ... παῖς θεοῦ; Origen from ᾠήθη
Matthew 19:6, 1 Corinthians 6:17, Colossians 1:15 and Plato, Letter 6, 323d checked; correct
